articles.title: Trump's super intelligence is rapidly catching up in the USA with 3X rise in search as Google Trends shows decreasing interest in 'Enemy' AI — while the rest of the world blissfully ignores it
articles.summary: The term “super intelligence” is growing in prominence in the US – but the rest of the world is sticking with “artificial intelligence”
articles.paragraph: In the US, Following the signing of Executive Order 14434, the purpose of which is “Inaugurating the Age of Super Intelligence,” the POTUS has taken to social media to emphasize the preferred term for artificial intelligence in the Land of the Free. While the rest of civilization continues with the term “artificial intelligence,” it seems the US public quite likes the term “super intelligence,” which is believed to have been introduced to cast AI in a more positive light. Since the executive order was passed, interest in the term “super intelligence” grew considerably, increasing by around three times at one point. Of course, this only happened in the USA - worldwide, attention was not drawn to the revised nomenclature.

articles.title: Niobia takes the guesswork out of some of tech’s most expensive mistakes
articles.summary: The San Francisco startup aims to help battery and chip manufacturers identify defects on production lines, reducing downtime and costly mistakes.
articles.paragraph: The San Francisco startup aims to help battery and chip manufacturers identify defects on production lines, reducing downtime and costly mistakes. Hardware Niobia takes the guesswork out of some of tech’s most expensive mistakes Zack Whittaker 12:00 PM PDT · October 13, 2026 San Francisco-based startup Niobia is betting big on a critical but often overlooked part of battery and chip making: helping engineers understand how and why things go wrong. Its AI software flags production defects and lets engineers ask a chatbot what caused them, aiming to deliver answers in minutes rather than days. How it works (broadly): The company’s customers place AI agents on their production lines to look for defects, then loop in human engineers to work out what might cause a product to fail.

articles.title: VisionQuest will show you an 'older and more mature' but still dangerous Ultron, star says
articles.summary: The man responsible for bringing Ultron to life in the MCU has teased what fans can expect from the returning villain.
articles.paragraph: The man responsible for bringing Ultron to life in the MCU has teased what fans can expect from the returning villain. Speaking exclusively to TechRadar at the series' UK junket, Spader teased how Ultron has evolved since his sole appearance in the Marvel Cinematic Universe (MCU), which came in 2014's Avengers: Age of Ultron. Back then, fans believed they'd seen the last of the genocidal android because — spoilers for a 12-year-old movie incoming — Ultron was destroyed. However, over a decade on from his apparent demise at Vision's hands, Ultron has returned, with a back-up copy of his source code retained by Vision in his mind — or, rather, his quantum processor. In the years that have followed, Ultron has been able to observe humanity and events in the MCU through Vision's eyes.

articles.title: Forget rockets — Longshot wants to fire cargo into space from a gun. See it at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026
articles.summary: Longshot is trying to build a gun big enough to make space data centers a reality.
articles.paragraph: Longshot is trying to build a gun big enough to make space data centers a reality. There are, at least in theory, other ways to do the job — space elevators, centrifuges, or a big chain hanging from a satellite in space and scooping up cargo from Earth. (Blue Origin spent some time thinking about that one before the idea wound up in a Neal Stephenson novel.) And then there’s an idea dating all the way back to Jules Verne: Use a big gun to shoot a projectile into space. Longshot Space Technology, a startup based in Alameda, California, is working on exactly that. The co-founders, CEO Mike Grace and CTO Nato Saichek, see an opportunity to take a technology that has already proven its worth and apply it to the pressing need for space launch.

articles.title: The ocean circulation that persists even after a key AMOC component fails
articles.summary: The Atlantic meridional overturning circulation (AMOC) is thought to face a potentially existential threat from climate change.
articles.paragraph: The Atlantic meridional overturning circulation (AMOC) is thought to face a potentially existential threat from climate change. But attempts to model what happens to AMOC as the oceans warm show divergent outcomes, leaving its fate unclear. In a paper published in AGU Advances, Shantong Sun and Andrew Thompson use a hierarchy of models to show that the cross-hemispheric overturning could persist for centuries even as North Atlantic Deep Water (NADW) formation shuts down.

articles.title: Satellite model finds Alpine peatlands may be smaller than official maps show
articles.summary: Peatlands in the Alps are mostly small, scattered and difficult to access. As a result, up-to-date information on their extent and condition is often lacking.
articles.paragraph: Peatlands in the Alps are mostly small, scattered and difficult to access. As a result, up-to-date information on their extent and condition is often lacking. An international research team, including researchers from the University of Göttingen, has now developed a cross-border approach to identifying these particular areas. A comparison with official maps shows that the model identifies many peatlands as smaller than previously mapped—particularly in areas where aerial photographs reveal visible signs of disturbance. The findings were published in the journal Communications Earth & Environme

articles.title: Newly discovered antiviral system in bacteria is 'strangest of its kind'
articles.summary: Researchers at Gladstone Institutes have uncovered an unusual bacterial immune system that operates in reverse of known defenses.
articles.paragraph: Researchers at Gladstone Institutes have uncovered an unusual bacterial immune system that operates in reverse of known defenses. The discovery, published in Molecular Cell, details the mechanics of "type VI retrons"—a counterintuitive class of bacterial defenses. More than just a biological curiosity, decoding these complex systems provides a molecular blueprint that scientists can adapt to engineer more efficient DNA-editing tools for human health and therapies.

articles.title: Before leaf miner damage shows, horse chestnut leaves alter how they function
articles.summary: Researchers from Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE) and Semmelweis University have investigated what happens to horse chestnut leaves when they are attacked from within by the horse chestnut leaf miner.
articles.paragraph: Researchers from Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE) and Semmelweis University have investigated what happens to horse chestnut leaves when they are attacked from within by the horse chestnut leaf miner. Their findings show that the functioning of the leaf changes while the damage is still barely visible to the naked eye. The results have been published in the journal Plant Stress.

articles.title: Bitcoin Whale That Sat Through Every Crash Since 2020 Just Moved $377M
articles.summary: A wallet that received 4,581 BTC in March 2020, worth about $40 million then, moved its stash today when it was worth about $377 million.
articles.paragraph: A wallet that received 4,581 BTC in March 2020, worth about $40 million then, moved its stash today when it was worth about $377 million. A Bitcoin wallet that has held 4,581.94 BTC since March 2020 sent its entire balance to five new addresses on Oct. 12, moving about $377 million in a single transaction, according to blockchain data. The transfer confirmed in block 971,126 at about 18:37 UTC, with Bitcoin trading around $82,350. Four of the receiving addresses got exactly 1,000 BTC each, and the fifth received 581.94 BTC. The transaction paid a fee of 732 satoshis, the hundred-millionth-of-a-bitcoin units known as sats, or about 60 cents. As of block 971,279 on Oct. 13, none of the five addresses has spent anything, and it is unclear who controls the wallet or where the coins are going.

articles.title: Strive Buys $280 Million in Bitcoin, Its Largest Purchase in Months
articles.summary: The Nasdaq-listed asset manager bought the Bitcoin at an average of about $84,500 during a rough week for the market, lifting its total stash to 32,773 BTC.
articles.paragraph: Strive scooped up another 3,311 BTC worth roughly $280 million in its biggest single purchase since January. Strive is piling into Bitcoin at its fastest clip of the year, scooping up another 3,311 BTC worth roughly $280 million in its biggest single purchase since January. The Nasdaq-listed asset manager, which trades under the ticker ASST, disclosed in a filing Monday that it bought the Bitcoin between Oct. 5 and Oct. 9 at an average price of about $84,500 per coin, including fees. The buy lifts Strive’s total holdings to 32,773 BTC, worth roughly $2.73 billion at today’s prices, up from 29,462 BTC a week earlier. The purchase caps a stretch of aggressive accumulation.

articles.title: AI Researchers Are Smoking Cigarettes to Prove AI Will Cure Cancer, Says Palantir Exec
articles.summary: Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar says many AI researchers have taken up smoking to signal their faith in AI.
articles.paragraph: Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar says many AI researchers have taken up smoking to signal their faith that AI will cure cancer. Nothing says "I trust the future of medicine" quite like lighting a Marlboro and waiting for the chatbot to fix your lungs. That is the habit Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar says is spreading among AI researchers, who have supposedly started smoking cigarettes to prove how confident they are that AI will cure cancer. "So many AI researchers have started smoking as a way of signaling to other researchers how much they believe in AI," Sankar said in an interview on CBS News' "Face the Nation" on Sunday. "I believe so much in AI that it's going to cure cancer. So I'm showing you my chips are all in." He did not name a single researcher, cite a survey, or explain how he knows.
